segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then I looked, and there was the Lamb, standing on Mount Zion, and with him a hundred and forty-four thousand who had his name and his Father’s name written on their foreheads.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I heard a sound from heaven like the sound of many waters and like the sound of loud thunder, and the sound I heard was like harpists playing on their harps.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they sing what seems a new song before the throne and before the four living creatures and the elders. No one could learn the song except the hundred and forty-four thousand, who have been bought from the earth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: These are the ones who have not defiled themselves with women, for they are virgins. These are the ones who follow the Lamb wherever he goes. These were bought from among humankind as firstfruits for God and for the Lamb,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and no lie was found in their mouth; they are blameless.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then I saw another angel flying high overhead, with eternal good news to announce to those who live on the earth, to every nation and tribe and language and people,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying in a loud voice,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Fear God and give him glory, for the hour of his judgment has come; and worship the one who made heaven and earth and sea and springs of water.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then another angel, a second, followed, saying,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great, who has made all the nations drink the wine of the fury of her prostitution.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then another angel, a third, followed them, saying in a loud voice,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “If anyone worships the beast and its image and receives a mark on their forehead or on their hand,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: that person too will drink the wine of God’s fury, poured undiluted into the cup of his wrath, and will be tormented with fire and sulfur before holy angels and before the Lamb.

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: And the smoke of their torment rises forever and ever, and they have no rest day or night, those who worship the beast and its image, and anyone who receives the mark of its name.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Here is the endurance of the holy ones, those who keep the commandments of God and their faith in Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I heard a voice from heaven saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Write this: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on.”

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Yes,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: says the Spirit,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “so that they may rest from their labors, for their deeds follow them.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then I looked, and there was a white cloud, and seated on the cloud was one like a son of man, with a golden crown on his head and a sharp sickle in his hand.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And another angel came out of the temple, crying out in a loud voice to the one seated on the cloud,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Put in your sickle and reap, for the hour to reap has come, because the harvest of the earth is fully ripe.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the one seated on the cloud swung his sickle over the earth, and the earth was reaped.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then another angel came out of the temple in heaven, and he too had a sharp sickle.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And another angel came from the altar, the one who has authority over the fire, and he called in a loud voice to the one who had the sharp sickle,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Put in your sharp sickle and gather the clusters from the vine of the earth, for its grapes are ripe.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the angel swung his sickle into the earth and gathered the vintage of the earth and threw it into the great winepress of God’s fury.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the winepress was trodden outside the city, and blood flowed from the winepress, as high as the horses’ bridles, for sixteen hundred stadia.

notes.note: The verb is the ordinary marketplace word for buying, the same one used just before (13:17) of those who cannot buy or sell without the beast’s mark. Most English versions render it “redeemed” here and in verse 4, which is theologically apt but hides both the plainness of the word and the echo. The image is of people purchased to belong to God.

The word is normally used of women, and its application to this company is striking. It can be read literally, of celibacy, or figuratively, of fidelity to God: the prophets regularly picture idolatry as sexual unfaithfulness, and this chapter goes on to speak of Babylon’s prostitution. Most interpreters take it figuratively, some seeing an allusion to the abstinence required of Israel’s soldiers on campaign, but the point is disputed.

The Greek word meant good news or a public announcement of it, and here it has no article and is paired with its own verb, “to announce good news.” Most translations use “gospel.” Interpreters differ on whether this is the Christian message as such or a specific summons, given in verse 7, to fear God as his judgment arrives.

The same Greek word, in the plural, is translated “Gentiles” elsewhere in this translation when it means the non-Jewish peoples. In Revelation’s lists of peoples, and in “all the nations” in verse 8, the scope is the whole world, so “nation” is used.

The cry echoes Isaiah 21:9. Babylon was the empire that destroyed Jerusalem and its temple in the sixth century BC; most scholars think the name here stands for Rome, which did the same in AD 70. Some read it more broadly as any imperial power set against God.

notes.phrase: the wine of the fury of her prostitution
notes.traditional: the wine of the wrath of her fornication
notes.note: The Greek word can mean either passion or anger. Many translations use “passion” here and “wrath” in verses 10 and 19; others think the wine is one that brings God’s wrath on those who drink it. “Fury” is used in all three places so that the echo is audible: those who drink Babylon’s wine will drink God’s. “Prostitution” replaces the traditional “fornication” because Babylon is later pictured as a prostitute, an image the prophets use for idolatry and corrupting alliances.

The Greek says literally “mixed unmixed.” Wine was normally mixed with water before drinking, and the verb for mixing had come to be used for preparing or pouring a drink. Undiluted wine is wine at full strength: the image is of judgment with nothing to soften it.

The traditional “saints” now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The Greek term is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God’s people.”

The Greek is literally “the faith of Jesus,” and “their” is supplied. Most translations understand it as faith in Jesus, as here. It could also mean faithfulness to Jesus, or the faithfulness that Jesus himself showed, to which they hold fast.

notes.phrase: one like a son of man
notes.traditional: one like unto the Son of man
notes.note: The phrase comes from Daniel 7:13, where “one like a son of man,” a Semitic way of saying a human figure, comes with the clouds of heaven; Revelation 1:13 uses it of the risen Christ. Most interpreters identify the figure here as Christ. A minority think an angel is meant, since “another angel” follows and gives him the command to reap.

notes.traditional: a thousand and six hundred furlongs
notes.note: A stadion was about 185 metres, so the distance is roughly 300 kilometres, or about 185 miles. Many interpreters think the figure is symbolic, since it is the square of four multiplied by the square of ten, but its exact significance is uncertain.

candidates.reason: Occurs throughout the New Testament and translators divide between “gospel” and “good news”; readers would be confused if chapters varied.
Revelation repeatedly pairs θυμός with ὀργή and plays on the wine of Babylon’s θυμός against God’s, so the two words need fixed, distinct English across chapters 14–19.
Recurs across the Gospels, Paul and Revelation with renderings ranging from “fornication” to “sexual immorality” to “prostitution”; the figurative use for Babylon needs to match chapters 17–19.
Used of Christ’s purchase of people (1 Corinthians 6:20; 2 Peter 2:1; Revelation 5:9) where tradition wavers between “bought” and “redeemed,” blurring the distinction from λυτρόω.
Very frequent in the Gospels and Revelation and ranges from physical prostration before a superior to worship of God; translators vary between “worship” and “bow down.”
